Title: Serum neurofilament light and tau as prognostic markers for all-cause mortality in the
elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study
Version: 0 Date: 02 Oct 2020
Reviewer's report:
The study of Rübsamen et al. report on the serum levels of neurofilament light chain (NfL) and tau
protein in a group of 385 elderly patients (>65 yrs.) included in the Memory and Morbidity in
Augsburg Elderly (MEMO) study. The serum levels of NfL and tau were measured using an
highly sensitive technique (single molecule array assays) and were compared with neuropsy-
chological tests and brain MRI result to asses the prognostic accuracy of the biomarkers for overall
mortality in elderly individuals without pre-defined neurological conditions.
1- In section Methods the difference between medium (3-10 mm diameter) or large (>10 mm)
white matter lesions (WML) and lacunar infarcts (defined as "hypodense (T1, PD) or hyperdense
(T2) lesion of a diameter between 3 and 15 mm") is not so clear.
2- No lacunar infarctions are reported in tab 1 while they are present in tab 2.
3- Serum NfL levels are correlated with axonal damage not only of the central nervous system but
also with axonal damage of the peripheral nervous system in acquired neuropathies (Mariotto et al.
2017), therefore the elevation of serum NfL may be due to peripheral neuropathy, whose
frequency progressively increases in the elderly population.
4- In Conclusions the sentence: "We found that both NfL and tau were associated with all-cause
mortality" must be changed because NfL and tau serum levels were associated with all-cause
mortality.
4- The present study demonstrated a predictive value of serum levels of NfL in all-cause mortality,
but does not correlate NfL levels with the different causes of death, in particular with mortality
associated with neurological disease.

Title: Serum neurofilament light and tau as prognostic markers for all-cause mortality in the
elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study
Version: 0 Date: 14 Oct 2020
Reviewer: Brian Gordon
Reviewer's report:
In the current work the authors retrospectively analyze blood samples take in 1997 as part of the
Memory and Morbidity in Augsburg elderly (MEMO). As part of MEMO participants underwent
neuropsychological testing and a subset had 1.5T MRI scans. They authors are interested in how
blood levels of NfL and tau are related to mortality, neuropsychological performance, and brain
atrophy and white matter lesions. The authors find that primarily NfL is related to mortality,
neuropsychological performance, and changes measured on MRI. The primary strength of the
current work is that it is being performed in a general population study and the length of follow-
up. Prior work has estimated the association of NfL, and even tau now, with MRI measures, but it
is still interesting to see what additional value can be gained by retrospectively adding new
biomarkers to a study. I have a number of points for clarification.
1.Could the authors provide more information about how WML are being quantified? The text
indicates they are being visually read. Is the reader selecting voxels that are abnormal which are
then quantified? My first thought is they were doing a reading like a Fazekas score but this seems
to be semiquantitative. You reference two prior papers from 2000 but a reader is unlikely to go
look those up to read. More information would be very helpful to the reader.
2.Given the slice thickness of your scans, how could you have WML less than 3mm in size? Also
you give the slice thickness, but not the in-plane resolution. This goes back to my first point that it
just was not clear to me how the WML values were being generated.
3.The authors start with a base model that includes age, sex, and education as predictors. They
then assess incremental models adding in additional factors of interest (e.g. NfL). Was there any
structure into how variables were entered into the model? This seems like an example were a
stepwise regression model would be appropriate, but it isn't clear what the authors did.
4.It was clear that you only imputed data when using MRI variables to predict mortality, but why
use imputation at all? What exact variables required imputation and how much of the data was
imputed? Are you imputing variables for all 117 individuals that do not have any MRI data? Did
you have enough data to actually impute any of your MRI variables accurately? Please clarify
what you did and provide justification. I may be more appropriate to simply perform the analyses
that include MRI only in the subset that actually has MRI data.

5.When performing the associations between tau/NfL and neuropsychological tests/MRI did you
include any covariates? Given the strong association NfL has with age, it would be appropriate to
include age a covariate.
6.I originally thought MRI was being summed into one aggregate measure for analyses, but it
looks like you analyzed the associations with individual regional measures as well. Did you adjust
for multiple comparisons?

Reviewer’s report
Title: Serum neurofilament light and tau as prognostic markers for all-cause mortality in the
elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study
Version: 0 Date: 07 Sep 2020
Reviewer's report:
I reviewed this manuscript that describes the evaluation of demographic, clinical, MRI and
biomarkers in a cohort of individuals recruited from the general population in the 1989/90s and
evaluated in detail in 1997.
The author focused on the group aged > 65y at the time of assessment, and evaluated the inter-
relationship between variables, and the value of baseline variables in predicting mortality.
Overall the manuscript is well written, clear and easy to follow. There are several strengths of the
paper:
- I agree with the authors that there is novelty in their findings
- The long follow up time
- The multi-dimensional data: demographic, clinical (including detailed cognitive), MRI and
biological data
- The correction of regressions for age, sex, years in education
- The high quality figures
However, I have some reservations and comments that I would like the authors to address to try to
strengthen the paper further.
- The MRI methods are unusual, which is almost certainly because the MR data is quite historic,
and was performed in a pre-digital era. However, I felt there was insufficient detail in the paper to
justify/ reproduce the methods. I was unclear how the size-dependent constant was derived and
whether this was subject to any validation. I could not access the Neuroepidemiology reference for
the cortical volume measurements, and suspect others will also be unable. I would therefore
recommend the authors provide more detail on that method and its validity (is it reproducible
between observers, has it ever been validated vs more modern quantitative volume metrics?). I
also found the term "atrophy" misleading as it implies volume change, whereas the authors had a
single scan for each participant. Please consider using a more appropriate description e.g. cortical
volume. Likewise there was reference to "change" at points (e.g. lines 209 and 260), which was
also misleading. I think these points could either be addressed, or they could be better recognised
as limitations.
- Overall the discussion seemed fairly limited and could be expanded. For example, could the
authors help the reader interpret the magnitude of the effect described by a c-statistic change from
0.663 to 0.683. Some further discussion on potential limitations including MRI (above), the
degree to which the research cohort are expected to be representative of the wider "general"
population, the relevance of the associations between tau and mortality in men vs women, the
interpretation of other researchers of sNfL in disease state (a explicit reminder that NfL is non-
specific - of course this is implied by the paper as a whole but I see that conclusion as a key take-
home message from this paper). Finally, why sNfL doesn't increase prognostic accuracy when

brain atrophy or neuropsych scores are included in models: do you feel that serum biomarkers are
more likely to be alternatives to MRI, or complementary to MRI in clinical studies? You touch on
this briefly, but the discussion could be developed a little.
- Minor typographical errors:
*Whilst the English is generally good and the paper is written clearly, there are a couple of places
with grammatical errors e.g. line 85, lines 95-98.
*Abstract says NfL HR of 1.26, but in results, line 244, and Figure 1 it says the risk of death
increased by 27%.

=== ReviewerReport_V0_R2 ===
Reviewer’s report
Title: Serum neurofilament light and tau as prognostic markers for all-cause mortality in the
elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study
Version: 0 Date: 18 Sep 2020
Reviewer's report:
The authors here analysed serum tau and NfL in a cohort of patients previously enrolled without
pre-defined neurological conditions. They compare tau/NfL levels with neuropsychological tests
and MRI parameters and assess their value as prognostic biomarkers for mortality. The authors
found an association between tau and NfL values and all-cause mortality and between NfL values
and neuropsychological tests score, brain atrophy, and white matter lesions.
Comments:
*Background:
-The authors state that "so far, serum NfL and tau have only been investigated for their prognostic
value in patient population while studies in the general population are missing". Actually, a couple
of studies analysed the prognostic value of NfL in patients without dementia (Mielke et al.
Neurology 2019 and de Wolf et al. Brain 2020), although focusing mainly on cognitive/
neuroimaging outcome. These should be cited and commented on the basis of the authors' data.
*Methods:
-Serum NfL are increased also in patients with peripheral neuropathies, which are quite common
in the elderly (Mariotto et al. J Peripher Nerv Syst 2018 and J Neurol 2020). Did the authors
consider/exclude this comorbidity?
-How did the authors differentiate medium/large WML and lacunar infarction (defined as a
hypodense OR hyperdense T2 lesion of 3-15 mm in diameter)? According to Table 1, none of the
participant had lacunar stroke, which seems unlikely and is not concordant with the association
reported between NfL levels and lacunar stroke (pg. 13 and Table 3).
-Why did the authors collect serum and plasma? Did they use only serum for the analysis or both?
And if they analysed serum or plasma, did they consider the possible difference of NfL values in
the two matrices?
Discussion
-In the last paragraph, the authors discuss the association between vascular changes at the time of
assessment and NfL levels. Actually, we are not able to date the onset of vascular lesions, and NfL
levels seem more reliable in measuring an ongoing/recent axonal damage. This should be
comment and discuss.

Reviewer’s report
Title: Serum neurofilament light and tau as prognostic markers for all-cause mortality in the
elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study
Version: 0 Date: 24 Sep 2020
Reviewer's report:
The present study links increased plasma concentrations of NfL and tau to increased risk of death.
The study is well phrased and the statistical analysis seems sound. However, the conclusions
reached seems of modest value both clinically and from a research standpoint. The methods
sections mentions that "death certificates were obtained" and hints that they were used to
categorize the deceased subjects in the study. But, from what I can find, this information is not
used in the study. Why is this? Increased NfL concentrations are known to be linked to
cerebrovascular disease, which in turn characterizes a subject with sever cardiovascular disease
and risk factors. It's not surprising that this would be associated with an increased mortality risk.
The authors need to discuss cause of death in relation to biomarker levels and better highlight the
value of the results reached, or at the very least acknowledge this lack of information as a
weakness of the study. They also need to defend, or better explain, the clinical value of the
conclusions reached.

Reviewer’s report
Title: Serum neurofilament light and tau as prognostic markers for all-cause mortality in the
elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study
Version: 0 Date: 02 Oct 2020
Reviewer's report:
The study of Rübsamen et al. report on the serum levels of neurofilament light chain (NfL) and tau
protein in a group of 385 elderly patients (>65 yrs.) included in the Memory and Morbidity in
Augsburg Elderly (MEMO) study. The serum levels of NfL and tau were measured using an
highly sensitive technique (single molecule array assays) and were compared with neuropsy-
chological tests and brain MRI result to asses the prognostic accuracy of the biomarkers for overall
mortality in elderly individuals without pre-defined neurological conditions.
1- In section Methods the difference between medium (3-10 mm diameter) or large (>10 mm)
white matter lesions (WML) and lacunar infarcts (defined as "hypodense (T1, PD) or hyperdense
(T2) lesion of a diameter between 3 and 15 mm") is not so clear.
2- No lacunar infarctions are reported in tab 1 while they are present in tab 2.
3- Serum NfL levels are correlated with axonal damage not only of the central nervous system but
also with axonal damage of the peripheral nervous system in acquired neuropathies (Mariotto et al.
2017), therefore the elevation of serum NfL may be due to peripheral neuropathy, whose
frequency progressively increases in the elderly population.
4- In Conclusions the sentence: "We found that both NfL and tau were associated with all-cause
mortality" must be changed because NfL and tau serum levels were associated with all-cause
mortality.
4- The present study demonstrated a predictive value of serum levels of NfL in all-cause mortality,
but does not correlate NfL levels with the different causes of death, in particular with mortality
associated with neurological disease.

Reviewer’s report
Title: Serum neurofilament light and tau as prognostic markers for all-cause mortality in the
elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study
Version: 0 Date: 14 Oct 2020
Reviewer: Brian Gordon
Reviewer's report:
In the current work the authors retrospectively analyze blood samples take in 1997 as part of the
Memory and Morbidity in Augsburg elderly (MEMO). As part of MEMO participants underwent
neuropsychological testing and a subset had 1.5T MRI scans. They authors are interested in how
blood levels of NfL and tau are related to mortality, neuropsychological performance, and brain
atrophy and white matter lesions. The authors find that primarily NfL is related to mortality,
neuropsychological performance, and changes measured on MRI. The primary strength of the
current work is that it is being performed in a general population study and the length of follow-
up. Prior work has estimated the association of NfL, and even tau now, with MRI measures, but it
is still interesting to see what additional value can be gained by retrospectively adding new
biomarkers to a study. I have a number of points for clarification.
1.Could the authors provide more information about how WML are being quantified? The text
indicates they are being visually read. Is the reader selecting voxels that are abnormal which are
then quantified? My first thought is they were doing a reading like a Fazekas score but this seems
to be semiquantitative. You reference two prior papers from 2000 but a reader is unlikely to go
look those up to read. More information would be very helpful to the reader.
2.Given the slice thickness of your scans, how could you have WML less than 3mm in size? Also
you give the slice thickness, but not the in-plane resolution. This goes back to my first point that it
just was not clear to me how the WML values were being generated.
3.The authors start with a base model that includes age, sex, and education as predictors. They
then assess incremental models adding in additional factors of interest (e.g. NfL). Was there any
structure into how variables were entered into the model? This seems like an example were a
stepwise regression model would be appropriate, but it isn't clear what the authors did.
4.It was clear that you only imputed data when using MRI variables to predict mortality, but why
use imputation at all? What exact variables required imputation and how much of the data was
imputed? Are you imputing variables for all 117 individuals that do not have any MRI data? Did
you have enough data to actually impute any of your MRI variables accurately? Please clarify
what you did and provide justification. I may be more appropriate to simply perform the analyses
that include MRI only in the subset that actually has MRI data.

5.When performing the associations between tau/NfL and neuropsychological tests/MRI did you
include any covariates? Given the strong association NfL has with age, it would be appropriate to
include age a covariate.
6.I originally thought MRI was being summed into one aggregate measure for analyses, but it
looks like you analyzed the associations with individual regional measures as well. Did you adjust
for multiple comparisons?

Title: Serum neurofilament light and tau as prognostic markers for all-cause mortality in the
elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study
Version: 0 Date: 07 Sep 2020
Reviewer's report:
I reviewed this manuscript that describes the evaluation of demographic, clinical, MRI and
biomarkers in a cohort of individuals recruited from the general population in the 1989/90s and
evaluated in detail in 1997.
The author focused on the group aged > 65y at the time of assessment, and evaluated the inter-
relationship between variables, and the value of baseline variables in predicting mortality.
Overall the manuscript is well written, clear and easy to follow. There are several strengths of the
paper:
- I agree with the authors that there is novelty in their findings
- The long follow up time
- The multi-dimensional data: demographic, clinical (including detailed cognitive), MRI and
biological data
- The correction of regressions for age, sex, years in education
- The high quality figures
However, I have some reservations and comments that I would like the authors to address to try to
strengthen the paper further.
- The MRI methods are unusual, which is almost certainly because the MR data is quite historic,
and was performed in a pre-digital era. However, I felt there was insufficient detail in the paper to
justify/ reproduce the methods. I was unclear how the size-dependent constant was derived and
whether this was subject to any validation. I could not access the Neuroepidemiology reference for
the cortical volume measurements, and suspect others will also be unable. I would therefore
recommend the authors provide more detail on that method and its validity (is it reproducible
between observers, has it ever been validated vs more modern quantitative volume metrics?). I
also found the term "atrophy" misleading as it implies volume change, whereas the authors had a
single scan for each participant. Please consider using a more appropriate description e.g. cortical
volume. Likewise there was reference to "change" at points (e.g. lines 209 and 260), which was
also misleading. I think these points could either be addressed, or they could be better recognised
as limitations.
- Overall the discussion seemed fairly limited and could be expanded. For example, could the
authors help the reader interpret the magnitude of the effect described by a c-statistic change from
0.663 to 0.683. Some further discussion on potential limitations including MRI (above), the
degree to which the research cohort are expected to be representative of the wider "general"
population, the relevance of the associations between tau and mortality in men vs women, the
interpretation of other researchers of sNfL in disease state (a explicit reminder that NfL is non-
specific - of course this is implied by the paper as a whole but I see that conclusion as a key take-
home message from this paper). Finally, why sNfL doesn't increase prognostic accuracy when

brain atrophy or neuropsych scores are included in models: do you feel that serum biomarkers are
more likely to be alternatives to MRI, or complementary to MRI in clinical studies? You touch on
this briefly, but the discussion could be developed a little.
- Minor typographical errors:
*Whilst the English is generally good and the paper is written clearly, there are a couple of places
with grammatical errors e.g. line 85, lines 95-98.
*Abstract says NfL HR of 1.26, but in results, line 244, and Figure 1 it says the risk of death
increased by 27%.

Title: Serum neurofilament light and tau as prognostic markers for all-cause mortality in the
elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study
Version: 0 Date: 18 Sep 2020
Reviewer's report:
The authors here analysed serum tau and NfL in a cohort of patients previously enrolled without
pre-defined neurological conditions. They compare tau/NfL levels with neuropsychological tests
and MRI parameters and assess their value as prognostic biomarkers for mortality. The authors
found an association between tau and NfL values and all-cause mortality and between NfL values
and neuropsychological tests score, brain atrophy, and white matter lesions.
Comments:
*Background:
-The authors state that "so far, serum NfL and tau have only been investigated for their prognostic
value in patient population while studies in the general population are missing". Actually, a couple
of studies analysed the prognostic value of NfL in patients without dementia (Mielke et al.
Neurology 2019 and de Wolf et al. Brain 2020), although focusing mainly on cognitive/
neuroimaging outcome. These should be cited and commented on the basis of the authors' data.
*Methods:
-Serum NfL are increased also in patients with peripheral neuropathies, which are quite common
in the elderly (Mariotto et al. J Peripher Nerv Syst 2018 and J Neurol 2020). Did the authors
consider/exclude this comorbidity?
-How did the authors differentiate medium/large WML and lacunar infarction (defined as a
hypodense OR hyperdense T2 lesion of 3-15 mm in diameter)? According to Table 1, none of the
participant had lacunar stroke, which seems unlikely and is not concordant with the association
reported between NfL levels and lacunar stroke (pg. 13 and Table 3).
-Why did the authors collect serum and plasma? Did they use only serum for the analysis or both?
And if they analysed serum or plasma, did they consider the possible difference of NfL values in
the two matrices?
Discussion
-In the last paragraph, the authors discuss the association between vascular changes at the time of
assessment and NfL levels. Actually, we are not able to date the onset of vascular lesions, and NfL
levels seem more reliable in measuring an ongoing/recent axonal damage. This should be
comment and discuss.

Reviewer's report:
The present study links increased plasma concentrations of NfL and tau to increased risk of death.
The study is well phrased and the statistical analysis seems sound. However, the conclusions
reached seems of modest value both clinically and from a research standpoint. The methods
sections mentions that "death certificates were obtained" and hints that they were used to
categorize the deceased subjects in the study. But, from what I can find, this information is not
used in the study. Why is this? Increased NfL concentrations are known to be linked to
cerebrovascular disease, which in turn characterizes a subject with sever cardiovascular disease
and risk factors. It's not surprising that this would be associated with an increased mortality risk.
The authors need to discuss cause of death in relation to biomarker levels and better highlight the
value of the results reached, or at the very least acknowledge this lack of information as a
weakness of the study. They also need to defend, or better explain, the clinical value of the
conclusions reached.

elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study
Version: 0 Date: 02 Oct 2020
Reviewer's report:
The study of Rübsamen et al. report on the serum levels of neurofilament light chain (NfL) and tau
protein in a group of 385 elderly patients (>65 yrs.) included in the Memory and Morbidity in
Augsburg Elderly (MEMO) study. The serum levels of NfL and tau were measured using an
highly sensitive technique (single molecule array assays) and were compared with neuropsy-
chological tests and brain MRI result to asses the prognostic accuracy of the biomarkers for overall
mortality in elderly individuals without pre-defined neurological conditions.
1- In section Methods the difference between medium (3-10 mm diameter) or large (>10 mm)
white matter lesions (WML) and lacunar infarcts (defined as "hypodense (T1, PD) or hyperdense
(T2) lesion of a diameter between 3 and 15 mm") is not so clear.
2- No lacunar infarctions are reported in tab 1 while they are present in tab 2.
3- Serum NfL levels are correlated with axonal damage not only of the central nervous system but
also with axonal damage of the peripheral nervous system in acquired neuropathies (Mariotto et al.
2017), therefore the elevation of serum NfL may be due to peripheral neuropathy, whose
frequency progressively increases in the elderly population.
4- In Conclusions the sentence: "We found that both NfL and tau were associated with all-cause
mortality" must be changed because NfL and tau serum levels were associated with all-cause
mortality.
4- The present study demonstrated a predictive value of serum levels of NfL in all-cause mortality,
but does not correlate NfL levels with the different causes of death, in particular with mortality
associated with neurological disease.

Title: Serum neurofilament light and tau as prognostic markers for all-cause mortality in the
elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study
Version: 0 Date: 14 Oct 2020
Reviewer: Brian Gordon
Reviewer's report:
In the current work the authors retrospectively analyze blood samples take in 1997 as part of the
Memory and Morbidity in Augsburg elderly (MEMO). As part of MEMO participants underwent
neuropsychological testing and a subset had 1.5T MRI scans. They authors are interested in how
blood levels of NfL and tau are related to mortality, neuropsychological performance, and brain
atrophy and white matter lesions. The authors find that primarily NfL is related to mortality,
neuropsychological performance, and changes measured on MRI. The primary strength of the
current work is that it is being performed in a general population study and the length of follow-
up. Prior work has estimated the association of NfL, and even tau now, with MRI measures, but it
is still interesting to see what additional value can be gained by retrospectively adding new
biomarkers to a study. I have a number of points for clarification.
1.Could the authors provide more information about how WML are being quantified? The text
indicates they are being visually read. Is the reader selecting voxels that are abnormal which are
then quantified? My first thought is they were doing a reading like a Fazekas score but this seems
to be semiquantitative. You reference two prior papers from 2000 but a reader is unlikely to go
look those up to read. More information would be very helpful to the reader.
2.Given the slice thickness of your scans, how could you have WML less than 3mm in size? Also
you give the slice thickness, but not the in-plane resolution. This goes back to my first point that it
just was not clear to me how the WML values were being generated.
3.The authors start with a base model that includes age, sex, and education as predictors. They
then assess incremental models adding in additional factors of interest (e.g. NfL). Was there any
structure into how variables were entered into the model? This seems like an example were a
stepwise regression model would be appropriate, but it isn't clear what the authors did.
4.It was clear that you only imputed data when using MRI variables to predict mortality, but why
use imputation at all? What exact variables required imputation and how much of the data was
imputed? Are you imputing variables for all 117 individuals that do not have any MRI data? Did
you have enough data to actually impute any of your MRI variables accurately? Please clarify
what you did and provide justification. I may be more appropriate to simply perform the analyses
that include MRI only in the subset that actually has MRI data.

5.When performing the associations between tau/NfL and neuropsychological tests/MRI did you
include any covariates? Given the strong association NfL has with age, it would be appropriate to
include age a covariate.
6.I originally thought MRI was being summed into one aggregate measure for analyses, but it
looks like you analyzed the associations with individual regional measures as well. Did you adjust
for multiple comparisons?

Reviewer’s report
Title: Serum neurofilament light and tau as prognostic markers for all-cause mortality in the
elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study
Version: 0 Date: 07 Sep 2020
Reviewer's report:
I reviewed this manuscript that describes the evaluation of demographic, clinical, MRI and
biomarkers in a cohort of individuals recruited from the general population in the 1989/90s and
evaluated in detail in 1997.
The author focused on the group aged > 65y at the time of assessment, and evaluated the inter-
relationship between variables, and the value of baseline variables in predicting mortality.
Overall the manuscript is well written, clear and easy to follow. There are several strengths of the
paper:
- I agree with the authors that there is novelty in their findings
- The long follow up time
- The multi-dimensional data: demographic, clinical (including detailed cognitive), MRI and
biological data
- The correction of regressions for age, sex, years in education
- The high quality figures
However, I have some reservations and comments that I would like the authors to address to try to
strengthen the paper further.
- The MRI methods are unusual, which is almost certainly because the MR data is quite historic,
and was performed in a pre-digital era. However, I felt there was insufficient detail in the paper to
justify/ reproduce the methods. I was unclear how the size-dependent constant was derived and
whether this was subject to any validation. I could not access the Neuroepidemiology reference for
the cortical volume measurements, and suspect others will also be unable. I would therefore
recommend the authors provide more detail on that method and its validity (is it reproducible
between observers, has it ever been validated vs more modern quantitative volume metrics?). I
also found the term "atrophy" misleading as it implies volume change, whereas the authors had a
single scan for each participant. Please consider using a more appropriate description e.g. cortical
volume. Likewise there was reference to "change" at points (e.g. lines 209 and 260), which was
also misleading. I think these points could either be addressed, or they could be better recognised
as limitations.
- Overall the discussion seemed fairly limited and could be expanded. For example, could the
authors help the reader interpret the magnitude of the effect described by a c-statistic change from
0.663 to 0.683. Some further discussion on potential limitations including MRI (above), the
degree to which the research cohort are expected to be representative of the wider "general"
population, the relevance of the associations between tau and mortality in men vs women, the
interpretation of other researchers of sNfL in disease state (a explicit reminder that NfL is non-
specific - of course this is implied by the paper as a whole but I see that conclusion as a key take-
home message from this paper). Finally, why sNfL doesn't increase prognostic accuracy when

brain atrophy or neuropsych scores are included in models: do you feel that serum biomarkers are
more likely to be alternatives to MRI, or complementary to MRI in clinical studies? You touch on
this briefly, but the discussion could be developed a little.
- Minor typographical errors:
*Whilst the English is generally good and the paper is written clearly, there are a couple of places
with grammatical errors e.g. line 85, lines 95-98.
*Abstract says NfL HR of 1.26, but in results, line 244, and Figure 1 it says the risk of death
increased by 27%.

Reviewer’s report
Title: Serum neurofilament light and tau as prognostic markers for all-cause mortality in the
elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study
Version: 0 Date: 18 Sep 2020
Reviewer's report:
The authors here analysed serum tau and NfL in a cohort of patients previously enrolled without
pre-defined neurological conditions. They compare tau/NfL levels with neuropsychological tests
and MRI parameters and assess their value as prognostic biomarkers for mortality. The authors
found an association between tau and NfL values and all-cause mortality and between NfL values
and neuropsychological tests score, brain atrophy, and white matter lesions.
Comments:
*Background:
-The authors state that "so far, serum NfL and tau have only been investigated for their prognostic
value in patient population while studies in the general population are missing". Actually, a couple
of studies analysed the prognostic value of NfL in patients without dementia (Mielke et al.
Neurology 2019 and de Wolf et al. Brain 2020), although focusing mainly on cognitive/
neuroimaging outcome. These should be cited and commented on the basis of the authors' data.
*Methods:
-Serum NfL are increased also in patients with peripheral neuropathies, which are quite common
in the elderly (Mariotto et al. J Peripher Nerv Syst 2018 and J Neurol 2020). Did the authors
consider/exclude this comorbidity?
-How did the authors differentiate medium/large WML and lacunar infarction (defined as a
hypodense OR hyperdense T2 lesion of 3-15 mm in diameter)? According to Table 1, none of the
participant had lacunar stroke, which seems unlikely and is not concordant with the association
reported between NfL levels and lacunar stroke (pg. 13 and Table 3).
-Why did the authors collect serum and plasma? Did they use only serum for the analysis or both?
And if they analysed serum or plasma, did they consider the possible difference of NfL values in
the two matrices?
Discussion
-In the last paragraph, the authors discuss the association between vascular changes at the time of
assessment and NfL levels. Actually, we are not able to date the onset of vascular lesions, and NfL
levels seem more reliable in measuring an ongoing/recent axonal damage. This should be
comment and discuss.

=== ReviewerReport_V0_R3 ===
Reviewer’s report
Title: Serum neurofilament light and tau as prognostic markers for all-cause mortality in the
elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study
Version: 0 Date: 24 Sep 2020
Reviewer's report:
The present study links increased plasma concentrations of NfL and tau to increased risk of death.
The study is well phrased and the statistical analysis seems sound. However, the conclusions
reached seems of modest value both clinically and from a research standpoint. The methods
sections mentions that "death certificates were obtained" and hints that they were used to
categorize the deceased subjects in the study. But, from what I can find, this information is not
used in the study. Why is this? Increased NfL concentrations are known to be linked to
cerebrovascular disease, which in turn characterizes a subject with sever cardiovascular disease
and risk factors. It's not surprising that this would be associated with an increased mortality risk.
The authors need to discuss cause of death in relation to biomarker levels and better highlight the
value of the results reached, or at the very least acknowledge this lack of information as a
weakness of the study. They also need to defend, or better explain, the clinical value of the
conclusions reached.

Reviewer’s report
Title: Serum neurofilament light and tau as prognostic markers for all-cause mortality in the
elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study
Version: 0 Date: 02 Oct 2020
Reviewer's report:
The study of Rübsamen et al. report on the serum levels of neurofilament light chain (NfL) and tau
protein in a group of 385 elderly patients (>65 yrs.) included in the Memory and Morbidity in
Augsburg Elderly (MEMO) study. The serum levels of NfL and tau were measured using an
highly sensitive technique (single molecule array assays) and were compared with neuropsy-
chological tests and brain MRI result to asses the prognostic accuracy of the biomarkers for overall
mortality in elderly individuals without pre-defined neurological conditions.
1- In section Methods the difference between medium (3-10 mm diameter) or large (>10 mm)
white matter lesions (WML) and lacunar infarcts (defined as "hypodense (T1, PD) or hyperdense
(T2) lesion of a diameter between 3 and 15 mm") is not so clear.
2- No lacunar infarctions are reported in tab 1 while they are present in tab 2.
3- Serum NfL levels are correlated with axonal damage not only of the central nervous system but
also with axonal damage of the peripheral nervous system in acquired neuropathies (Mariotto et al.
2017), therefore the elevation of serum NfL may be due to peripheral neuropathy, whose
frequency progressively increases in the elderly population.
4- In Conclusions the sentence: "We found that both NfL and tau were associated with all-cause
mortality" must be changed because NfL and tau serum levels were associated with all-cause
mortality.
4- The present study demonstrated a predictive value of serum levels of NfL in all-cause mortality,
but does not correlate NfL levels with the different causes of death, in particular with mortality
associated with neurological disease.

=== ReviewerReport_V0_R4 ===
Reviewer’s report
Title: Serum neurofilament light and tau as prognostic markers for all-cause mortality in the
elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study
Version: 0 Date: 14 Oct 2020
Reviewer: Brian Gordon
Reviewer's report:
In the current work the authors retrospectively analyze blood samples take in 1997 as part of the
Memory and Morbidity in Augsburg elderly (MEMO). As part of MEMO participants underwent
neuropsychological testing and a subset had 1.5T MRI scans. They authors are interested in how
blood levels of NfL and tau are related to mortality, neuropsychological performance, and brain
atrophy and white matter lesions. The authors find that primarily NfL is related to mortality,
neuropsychological performance, and changes measured on MRI. The primary strength of the
current work is that it is being performed in a general population study and the length of follow-
up. Prior work has estimated the association of NfL, and even tau now, with MRI measures, but it
is still interesting to see what additional value can be gained by retrospectively adding new
biomarkers to a study. I have a number of points for clarification.
1.Could the authors provide more information about how WML are being quantified? The text
indicates they are being visually read. Is the reader selecting voxels that are abnormal which are
then quantified? My first thought is they were doing a reading like a Fazekas score but this seems
to be semiquantitative. You reference two prior papers from 2000 but a reader is unlikely to go
look those up to read. More information would be very helpful to the reader.
2.Given the slice thickness of your scans, how could you have WML less than 3mm in size? Also
you give the slice thickness, but not the in-plane resolution. This goes back to my first point that it
just was not clear to me how the WML values were being generated.
3.The authors start with a base model that includes age, sex, and education as predictors. They
then assess incremental models adding in additional factors of interest (e.g. NfL). Was there any
structure into how variables were entered into the model? This seems like an example were a
stepwise regression model would be appropriate, but it isn't clear what the authors did.
4.It was clear that you only imputed data when using MRI variables to predict mortality, but why
use imputation at all? What exact variables required imputation and how much of the data was
imputed? Are you imputing variables for all 117 individuals that do not have any MRI data? Did
you have enough data to actually impute any of your MRI variables accurately? Please clarify
what you did and provide justification. I may be more appropriate to simply perform the analyses
that include MRI only in the subset that actually has MRI data.

5.When performing the associations between tau/NfL and neuropsychological tests/MRI did you
include any covariates? Given the strong association NfL has with age, it would be appropriate to
include age a covariate.
6.I originally thought MRI was being summed into one aggregate measure for analyses, but it
looks like you analyzed the associations with individual regional measures as well. Did you adjust
for multiple comparisons?

Title: Serum neurofilament light and tau as prognostic markers for all-cause mortality in the
elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study
Version: 0 Date: 07 Sep 2020
Reviewer's report:
I reviewed this manuscript that describes the evaluation of demographic, clinical, MRI and
biomarkers in a cohort of individuals recruited from the general population in the 1989/90s and
evaluated in detail in 1997.
The author focused on the group aged > 65y at the time of assessment, and evaluated the inter-
relationship between variables, and the value of baseline variables in predicting mortality.
Overall the manuscript is well written, clear and easy to follow. There are several strengths of the
paper:
- I agree with the authors that there is novelty in their findings
- The long follow up time
- The multi-dimensional data: demographic, clinical (including detailed cognitive), MRI and
biological data
- The correction of regressions for age, sex, years in education
- The high quality figures
However, I have some reservations and comments that I would like the authors to address to try to
strengthen the paper further.
- The MRI methods are unusual, which is almost certainly because the MR data is quite historic,
and was performed in a pre-digital era. However, I felt there was insufficient detail in the paper to
justify/ reproduce the methods. I was unclear how the size-dependent constant was derived and
whether this was subject to any validation. I could not access the Neuroepidemiology reference for
the cortical volume measurements, and suspect others will also be unable. I would therefore
recommend the authors provide more detail on that method and its validity (is it reproducible
between observers, has it ever been validated vs more modern quantitative volume metrics?). I
also found the term "atrophy" misleading as it implies volume change, whereas the authors had a
single scan for each participant. Please consider using a more appropriate description e.g. cortical
volume. Likewise there was reference to "change" at points (e.g. lines 209 and 260), which was
also misleading. I think these points could either be addressed, or they could be better recognised
as limitations.
- Overall the discussion seemed fairly limited and could be expanded. For example, could the
authors help the reader interpret the magnitude of the effect described by a c-statistic change from
0.663 to 0.683. Some further discussion on potential limitations including MRI (above), the
degree to which the research cohort are expected to be representative of the wider "general"
population, the relevance of the associations between tau and mortality in men vs women, the
interpretation of other researchers of sNfL in disease state (a explicit reminder that NfL is non-
specific - of course this is implied by the paper as a whole but I see that conclusion as a key take-
home message from this paper). Finally, why sNfL doesn't increase prognostic accuracy when

brain atrophy or neuropsych scores are included in models: do you feel that serum biomarkers are
more likely to be alternatives to MRI, or complementary to MRI in clinical studies? You touch on
this briefly, but the discussion could be developed a little.
- Minor typographical errors:
*Whilst the English is generally good and the paper is written clearly, there are a couple of places
with grammatical errors e.g. line 85, lines 95-98.
*Abstract says NfL HR of 1.26, but in results, line 244, and Figure 1 it says the risk of death
increased by 27%.

Title: Serum neurofilament light and tau as prognostic markers for all-cause mortality in the
elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study
Version: 0 Date: 18 Sep 2020
Reviewer's report:
The authors here analysed serum tau and NfL in a cohort of patients previously enrolled without
pre-defined neurological conditions. They compare tau/NfL levels with neuropsychological tests
and MRI parameters and assess their value as prognostic biomarkers for mortality. The authors
found an association between tau and NfL values and all-cause mortality and between NfL values
and neuropsychological tests score, brain atrophy, and white matter lesions.
Comments:
*Background:
-The authors state that "so far, serum NfL and tau have only been investigated for their prognostic
value in patient population while studies in the general population are missing". Actually, a couple
of studies analysed the prognostic value of NfL in patients without dementia (Mielke et al.
Neurology 2019 and de Wolf et al. Brain 2020), although focusing mainly on cognitive/
neuroimaging outcome. These should be cited and commented on the basis of the authors' data.
*Methods:
-Serum NfL are increased also in patients with peripheral neuropathies, which are quite common
in the elderly (Mariotto et al. J Peripher Nerv Syst 2018 and J Neurol 2020). Did the authors
consider/exclude this comorbidity?
-How did the authors differentiate medium/large WML and lacunar infarction (defined as a
hypodense OR hyperdense T2 lesion of 3-15 mm in diameter)? According to Table 1, none of the
participant had lacunar stroke, which seems unlikely and is not concordant with the association
reported between NfL levels and lacunar stroke (pg. 13 and Table 3).
-Why did the authors collect serum and plasma? Did they use only serum for the analysis or both?
And if they analysed serum or plasma, did they consider the possible difference of NfL values in
the two matrices?
Discussion
-In the last paragraph, the authors discuss the association between vascular changes at the time of
assessment and NfL levels. Actually, we are not able to date the onset of vascular lesions, and NfL
levels seem more reliable in measuring an ongoing/recent axonal damage. This should be
comment and discuss.

Version: 0 Date: 24 Sep 2020
Reviewer's report:
The present study links increased plasma concentrations of NfL and tau to increased risk of death.
The study is well phrased and the statistical analysis seems sound. However, the conclusions
reached seems of modest value both clinically and from a research standpoint. The methods
sections mentions that "death certificates were obtained" and hints that they were used to
categorize the deceased subjects in the study. But, from what I can find, this information is not
used in the study. Why is this? Increased NfL concentrations are known to be linked to
cerebrovascular disease, which in turn characterizes a subject with sever cardiovascular disease
and risk factors. It's not surprising that this would be associated with an increased mortality risk.

value of the results reached, or at the very least acknowledge this lack of information as a

elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study
Version: 0 Date: 02 Oct 2020
Reviewer's report:
The study of Rübsamen et al. report on the serum levels of neurofilament light chain (NfL) and tau
protein in a group of 385 elderly patients (>65 yrs.) included in the Memory and Morbidity in
Augsburg Elderly (MEMO) study. The serum levels of NfL and tau were measured using an
highly sensitive technique (single molecule array assays) and were compared with neuropsy-
chological tests and brain MRI result to asses the prognostic accuracy of the biomarkers for overall
mortality in elderly individuals without pre-defined neurological conditions.
1- In section Methods the difference between medium (3-10 mm diameter) or large (>10 mm)
white matter lesions (WML) and lacunar infarcts (defined as "hypodense (T1, PD) or hyperdense
(T2) lesion of a diameter between 3 and 15 mm") is not so clear.
2- No lacunar infarctions are reported in tab 1 while they are present in tab 2.
3- Serum NfL levels are correlated with axonal damage not only of the central nervous system but
also with axonal damage of the peripheral nervous system in acquired neuropathies (Mariotto et al.
2017), therefore the elevation of serum NfL may be due to peripheral neuropathy, whose
frequency progressively increases in the elderly population.
4- In Conclusions the sentence: "We found that both NfL and tau were associated with all-cause
mortality" must be changed because NfL and tau serum levels were associated with all-cause
mortality.
4- The present study demonstrated a predictive value of serum levels of NfL in all-cause mortality,
but does not correlate NfL levels with the different causes of death, in particular with mortality
associated with neurological disease.

Title: Serum neurofilament light and tau as prognostic markers for all-cause mortality in the
elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study
Version: 0 Date: 14 Oct 2020
Reviewer: Brian Gordon
Reviewer's report:
In the current work the authors retrospectively analyze blood samples take in 1997 as part of the
Memory and Morbidity in Augsburg elderly (MEMO). As part of MEMO participants underwent
neuropsychological testing and a subset had 1.5T MRI scans. They authors are interested in how
blood levels of NfL and tau are related to mortality, neuropsychological performance, and brain
atrophy and white matter lesions. The authors find that primarily NfL is related to mortality,
neuropsychological performance, and changes measured on MRI. The primary strength of the
current work is that it is being performed in a general population study and the length of follow-
up. Prior work has estimated the association of NfL, and even tau now, with MRI measures, but it
is still interesting to see what additional value can be gained by retrospectively adding new
biomarkers to a study. I have a number of points for clarification.
1.Could the authors provide more information about how WML are being quantified? The text
indicates they are being visually read. Is the reader selecting voxels that are abnormal which are
then quantified? My first thought is they were doing a reading like a Fazekas score but this seems
to be semiquantitative. You reference two prior papers from 2000 but a reader is unlikely to go
look those up to read. More information would be very helpful to the reader.
2.Given the slice thickness of your scans, how could you have WML less than 3mm in size? Also
you give the slice thickness, but not the in-plane resolution. This goes back to my first point that it
just was not clear to me how the WML values were being generated.
3.The authors start with a base model that includes age, sex, and education as predictors. They
then assess incremental models adding in additional factors of interest (e.g. NfL). Was there any
structure into how variables were entered into the model? This seems like an example were a
stepwise regression model would be appropriate, but it isn't clear what the authors did.
4.It was clear that you only imputed data when using MRI variables to predict mortality, but why
use imputation at all? What exact variables required imputation and how much of the data was
imputed? Are you imputing variables for all 117 individuals that do not have any MRI data? Did
you have enough data to actually impute any of your MRI variables accurately? Please clarify
what you did and provide justification. I may be more appropriate to simply perform the analyses
that include MRI only in the subset that actually has MRI data.

5.When performing the associations between tau/NfL and neuropsychological tests/MRI did you
include any covariates? Given the strong association NfL has with age, it would be appropriate to
include age a covariate.
6.I originally thought MRI was being summed into one aggregate measure for analyses, but it
looks like you analyzed the associations with individual regional measures as well. Did you adjust
for multiple comparisons?

Reviewer’s report
Title: Serum neurofilament light and tau as prognostic markers for all-cause mortality in the
elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study
Version: 0 Date: 07 Sep 2020
Reviewer's report:
I reviewed this manuscript that describes the evaluation of demographic, clinical, MRI and
biomarkers in a cohort of individuals recruited from the general population in the 1989/90s and
evaluated in detail in 1997.
The author focused on the group aged > 65y at the time of assessment, and evaluated the inter-
relationship between variables, and the value of baseline variables in predicting mortality.
Overall the manuscript is well written, clear and easy to follow. There are several strengths of the
paper:
- I agree with the authors that there is novelty in their findings
- The long follow up time
- The multi-dimensional data: demographic, clinical (including detailed cognitive), MRI and
biological data
- The correction of regressions for age, sex, years in education
- The high quality figures
However, I have some reservations and comments that I would like the authors to address to try to
strengthen the paper further.
- The MRI methods are unusual, which is almost certainly because the MR data is quite historic,
and was performed in a pre-digital era. However, I felt there was insufficient detail in the paper to
justify/ reproduce the methods. I was unclear how the size-dependent constant was derived and
whether this was subject to any validation. I could not access the Neuroepidemiology reference for
the cortical volume measurements, and suspect others will also be unable. I would therefore
recommend the authors provide more detail on that method and its validity (is it reproducible
between observers, has it ever been validated vs more modern quantitative volume metrics?). I
also found the term "atrophy" misleading as it implies volume change, whereas the authors had a
single scan for each participant. Please consider using a more appropriate description e.g. cortical
volume. Likewise there was reference to "change" at points (e.g. lines 209 and 260), which was
also misleading. I think these points could either be addressed, or they could be better recognised
as limitations.
- Overall the discussion seemed fairly limited and could be expanded. For example, could the
authors help the reader interpret the magnitude of the effect described by a c-statistic change from
0.663 to 0.683. Some further discussion on potential limitations including MRI (above), the
degree to which the research cohort are expected to be representative of the wider "general"
population, the relevance of the associations between tau and mortality in men vs women, the
interpretation of other researchers of sNfL in disease state (a explicit reminder that NfL is non-
specific - of course this is implied by the paper as a whole but I see that conclusion as a key take-
home message from this paper). Finally, why sNfL doesn't increase prognostic accuracy when

brain atrophy or neuropsych scores are included in models: do you feel that serum biomarkers are
more likely to be alternatives to MRI, or complementary to MRI in clinical studies? You touch on
this briefly, but the discussion could be developed a little.
- Minor typographical errors:
*Whilst the English is generally good and the paper is written clearly, there are a couple of places
with grammatical errors e.g. line 85, lines 95-98.
*Abstract says NfL HR of 1.26, but in results, line 244, and Figure 1 it says the risk of death
increased by 27%.

=== ReviewerReport_V0_R2 ===
Reviewer’s report
Title: Serum neurofilament light and tau as prognostic markers for all-cause mortality in the
elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study
Version: 0 Date: 18 Sep 2020
Reviewer's report:
The authors here analysed serum tau and NfL in a cohort of patients previously enrolled without
pre-defined neurological conditions. They compare tau/NfL levels with neuropsychological tests
and MRI parameters and assess their value as prognostic biomarkers for mortality. The authors
found an association between tau and NfL values and all-cause mortality and between NfL values
and neuropsychological tests score, brain atrophy, and white matter lesions.
Comments:
*Background:
-The authors state that "so far, serum NfL and tau have only been investigated for their prognostic
value in patient population while studies in the general population are missing". Actually, a couple
of studies analysed the prognostic value of NfL in patients without dementia (Mielke et al.
Neurology 2019 and de Wolf et al. Brain 2020), although focusing mainly on cognitive/
neuroimaging outcome. These should be cited and commented on the basis of the authors' data.
*Methods:
-Serum NfL are increased also in patients with peripheral neuropathies, which are quite common
in the elderly (Mariotto et al. J Peripher Nerv Syst 2018 and J Neurol 2020). Did the authors
consider/exclude this comorbidity?
-How did the authors differentiate medium/large WML and lacunar infarction (defined as a
hypodense OR hyperdense T2 lesion of 3-15 mm in diameter)? According to Table 1, none of the
participant had lacunar stroke, which seems unlikely and is not concordant with the association
reported between NfL levels and lacunar stroke (pg. 13 and Table 3).
-Why did the authors collect serum and plasma? Did they use only serum for the analysis or both?
And if they analysed serum or plasma, did they consider the possible difference of NfL values in
the two matrices?
Discussion
-In the last paragraph, the authors discuss the association between vascular changes at the time of
assessment and NfL levels. Actually, we are not able to date the onset of vascular lesions, and NfL
levels seem more reliable in measuring an ongoing/recent axonal damage. This should be
comment and discuss.

Reviewer’s report
Title: Serum neurofilament light and tau as prognostic markers for all-cause mortality in the
elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study
Version: 0 Date: 24 Sep 2020
Reviewer's report:
The present study links increased plasma concentrations of NfL and tau to increased risk of death.
The study is well phrased and the statistical analysis seems sound. However, the conclusions
reached seems of modest value both clinically and from a research standpoint. The methods
sections mentions that "death certificates were obtained" and hints that they were used to
categorize the deceased subjects in the study. But, from what I can find, this information is not
used in the study. Why is this? Increased NfL concentrations are known to be linked to
cerebrovascular disease, which in turn characterizes a subject with sever cardiovascular disease
and risk factors. It's not surprising that this would be associated with an increased mortality risk.
The authors need to discuss cause of death in relation to biomarker levels and better highlight the
value of the results reached, or at the very least acknowledge this lack of information as a
weakness of the study. They also need to defend, or better explain, the clinical value of the
conclusions reached.

Reviewer’s report
Title: Serum neurofilament light and tau as prognostic markers for all-cause mortality in the
elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study
Version: 0 Date: 02 Oct 2020
Reviewer's report:
The study of Rübsamen et al. report on the serum levels of neurofilament light chain (NfL) and tau
protein in a group of 385 elderly patients (>65 yrs.) included in the Memory and Morbidity in
Augsburg Elderly (MEMO) study. The serum levels of NfL and tau were measured using an
highly sensitive technique (single molecule array assays) and were compared with neuropsy-
chological tests and brain MRI result to asses the prognostic accuracy of the biomarkers for overall
mortality in elderly individuals without pre-defined neurological conditions.
1- In section Methods the difference between medium (3-10 mm diameter) or large (>10 mm)
white matter lesions (WML) and lacunar infarcts (defined as "hypodense (T1, PD) or hyperdense
(T2) lesion of a diameter between 3 and 15 mm") is not so clear.
2- No lacunar infarctions are reported in tab 1 while they are present in tab 2.
3- Serum NfL levels are correlated with axonal damage not only of the central nervous system but
also with axonal damage of the peripheral nervous system in acquired neuropathies (Mariotto et al.
2017), therefore the elevation of serum NfL may be due to peripheral neuropathy, whose
frequency progressively increases in the elderly population.
4- In Conclusions the sentence: "We found that both NfL and tau were associated with all-cause
mortality" must be changed because NfL and tau serum levels were associated with all-cause
mortality.
4- The present study demonstrated a predictive value of serum levels of NfL in all-cause mortality,
but does not correlate NfL levels with the different causes of death, in particular with mortality
associated with neurological disease.

Reviewer’s report
Title: Serum neurofilament light and tau as prognostic markers for all-cause mortality in the
elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study
Version: 0 Date: 14 Oct 2020
Reviewer: Brian Gordon
Reviewer's report:
In the current work the authors retrospectively analyze blood samples take in 1997 as part of the
Memory and Morbidity in Augsburg elderly (MEMO). As part of MEMO participants underwent
neuropsychological testing and a subset had 1.5T MRI scans. They authors are interested in how
blood levels of NfL and tau are related to mortality, neuropsychological performance, and brain
atrophy and white matter lesions. The authors find that primarily NfL is related to mortality,
neuropsychological performance, and changes measured on MRI. The primary strength of the
current work is that it is being performed in a general population study and the length of follow-
up. Prior work has estimated the association of NfL, and even tau now, with MRI measures, but it
is still interesting to see what additional value can be gained by retrospectively adding new
biomarkers to a study. I have a number of points for clarification.
1.Could the authors provide more information about how WML are being quantified? The text
indicates they are being visually read. Is the reader selecting voxels that are abnormal which are
then quantified? My first thought is they were doing a reading like a Fazekas score but this seems
to be semiquantitative. You reference two prior papers from 2000 but a reader is unlikely to go
look those up to read. More information would be very helpful to the reader.
2.Given the slice thickness of your scans, how could you have WML less than 3mm in size? Also
you give the slice thickness, but not the in-plane resolution. This goes back to my first point that it
just was not clear to me how the WML values were being generated.
3.The authors start with a base model that includes age, sex, and education as predictors. They
then assess incremental models adding in additional factors of interest (e.g. NfL). Was there any
structure into how variables were entered into the model? This seems like an example were a
stepwise regression model would be appropriate, but it isn't clear what the authors did.
4.It was clear that you only imputed data when using MRI variables to predict mortality, but why
use imputation at all? What exact variables required imputation and how much of the data was
imputed? Are you imputing variables for all 117 individuals that do not have any MRI data? Did
you have enough data to actually impute any of your MRI variables accurately? Please clarify
what you did and provide justification. I may be more appropriate to simply perform the analyses
that include MRI only in the subset that actually has MRI data.

5.When performing the associations between tau/NfL and neuropsychological tests/MRI did you
include any covariates? Given the strong association NfL has with age, it would be appropriate to
include age a covariate.
6.I originally thought MRI was being summed into one aggregate measure for analyses, but it
looks like you analyzed the associations with individual regional measures as well. Did you adjust
for multiple comparisons?

{"kind": "bmc_peer_review_reports", "parts": {"assets": [{"content_type": "application/pdf", "label": "ReviewerReport_V0_R1", "raw_path": "data_5000/raw/bmc_medicine/2021/10_1186_s12916_021_01915_8/official_review_asset_1.pdf", "status": "collected", "text": "Reviewer’s report
Title: Serum neurofilament light and tau as prognostic markers for all-cause mortality in the
elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study
Version: 0 Date: 07 Sep 2020
Reviewer's report:
I reviewed this manuscript that describes the evaluation of demographic, clinical, MRI and
biomarkers in a cohort of individuals recruited from the general population in the 1989/90s and
evaluated in detail in 1997.
The author focused on the group aged > 65y at the time of assessment, and evaluated the inter-
relationship between variables, and the value of baseline variables in predicting mortality.
Overall the manuscript is well written, clear and easy to follow. There are several strengths of the
paper:
- I agree with the authors that there is novelty in their findings
- The long follow up time
- The multi-dimensional data: demographic, clinical (including detailed cognitive), MRI and
biological data
- The correction of regressions for age, sex, years in education
- The high quality figures
However, I have some reservations and comments that I would like the authors to address to try to
strengthen the paper further.
- The MRI methods are unusual, which is almost certainly because the MR data is quite historic,
and was performed in a pre-digital era. However, I felt there was insufficient detail in the paper to
justify/ reproduce the methods. I was unclear how the size-dependent constant was derived and
whether this was subject to any validation. I could not access the Neuroepidemiology reference for
the cortical volume measurements, and suspect others will also be unable. I would therefore
recommend the authors provide more detail on that method and its validity (is it reproducible
between observers, has it ever been validated vs more modern quantitative volume metrics?). I
also found the term "atrophy" misleading as it implies volume change, whereas the authors had a
single scan for each participant. Please consider using a more appropriate description e.g. cortical
volume. Likewise there was reference to "change" at points (e.g. lines 209 and 260), which was
also misleading. I think these points could either be addressed, or they could be better recognised
as limitations.
- Overall the discussion seemed fairly limited and could be expanded. For example, could the
authors help the reader interpret the magnitude of the effect described by a c-statistic change from
0.663 to 0.683. Some further discussion on potential limitations including MRI (above), the
degree to which the research cohort are expected to be representative of the wider "general"
population, the relevance of the associations between tau and mortality in men vs women, the
interpretation of other researchers of sNfL in disease state (a explicit reminder that NfL is non-
specific - of course this is implied by the paper as a whole but I see that conclusion as a key take-
home message from this paper). Finally, why sNfL doesn't increase prognostic accuracy when

brain atrophy or neuropsych scores are included in models: do you feel that serum biomarkers are
more likely to be alternatives to MRI, or complementary to MRI in clinical studies? You touch on
this briefly, but the discussion could be developed a little.
- Minor typographical errors:
*Whilst the English is generally good and the paper is written clearly, there are a couple of places
with grammatical errors e.g. line 85, lines 95-98.
*Abstract says NfL HR of 1.26, but in results, line 244, and Figure 1 it says the risk of death
increased by 27%.

Title: Serum neurofilament light and tau as prognostic markers for all-cause mortality in the
elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study
Version: 0 Date: 18 Sep 2020
Reviewer's report:
The authors here analysed serum tau and NfL in a cohort of patients previously enrolled without
pre-defined neurological conditions. They compare tau/NfL levels with neuropsychological tests
and MRI parameters and assess their value as prognostic biomarkers for mortality. The authors
found an association between tau and NfL values and all-cause mortality and between NfL values
and neuropsychological tests score, brain atrophy, and white matter lesions.
Comments:
*Background:
-The authors state that "so far, serum NfL and tau have only been investigated for their prognostic
value in patient population while studies in the general population are missing". Actually, a couple
of studies analysed the prognostic value of NfL in patients without dementia (Mielke et al.
Neurology 2019 and de Wolf et al. Brain 2020), although focusing mainly on cognitive/
neuroimaging outcome. These should be cited and commented on the basis of the authors' data.
*Methods:
-Serum NfL are increased also in patients with peripheral neuropathies, which are quite common
in the elderly (Mariotto et al. J Peripher Nerv Syst 2018 and J Neurol 2020). Did the authors
consider/exclude this comorbidity?
-How did the authors differentiate medium/large WML and lacunar infarction (defined as a
hypodense OR hyperdense T2 lesion of 3-15 mm in diameter)? According to Table 1, none of the
participant had lacunar stroke, which seems unlikely and is not concordant with the association
reported between NfL levels and lacunar stroke (pg. 13 and Table 3).
-Why did the authors collect serum and plasma? Did they use only serum for the analysis or both?
And if they analysed serum or plasma, did they consider the possible difference of NfL values in
the two matrices?
Discussion
-In the last paragraph, the authors discuss the association between vascular changes at the time of
assessment and NfL levels. Actually, we are not able to date the onset of vascular lesions, and NfL
levels seem more reliable in measuring an ongoing/recent axonal damage. This should be
comment and discuss.

Reviewer's report:
The present study links increased plasma concentrations of NfL and tau to increased risk of death.
The study is well phrased and the statistical analysis seems sound. However, the conclusions
reached seems of modest value both clinically and from a research standpoint. The methods
sections mentions that "death certificates were obtained" and hints that they were used to
categorize the deceased subjects in the study. But, from what I can find, this information is not
used in the study. Why is this? Increased NfL concentrations are known to be linked to
cerebrovascular disease, which in turn characterizes a subject with sever cardiovascular disease
and risk factors. It's not surprising that this would be associated with an increased mortality risk.
The authors need to discuss cause of death in relation to biomarker levels and better highlight the
value of the results reached, or at the very least acknowledge this lack of information as a
weakness of the study. They also need to defend, or better explain, the clinical value of the
conclusions reached.

Reviewer's report:
The study of Rübsamen et al. report on the serum levels of neurofilament light chain (NfL) and tau
protein in a group of 385 elderly patients (>65 yrs.) included in the Memory and Morbidity in
Augsburg Elderly (MEMO) study. The serum levels of NfL and tau were measured using an
highly sensitive technique (single molecule array assays) and were compared with neuropsy-
chological tests and brain MRI result to asses the prognostic accuracy of the biomarkers for overall
mortality in elderly individuals without pre-defined neurological conditions.
1- In section Methods the difference between medium (3-10 mm diameter) or large (>10 mm)
white matter lesions (WML) and lacunar infarcts (defined as "hypodense (T1, PD) or hyperdense
(T2) lesion of a diameter between 3 and 15 mm") is not so clear.
2- No lacunar infarctions are reported in tab 1 while they are present in tab 2.
3- Serum NfL levels are correlated with axonal damage not only of the central nervous system but
also with axonal damage of the peripheral nervous system in acquired neuropathies (Mariotto et al.
2017), therefore the elevation of serum NfL may be due to peripheral neuropathy, whose
frequency progressively increases in the elderly population.
4- In Conclusions the sentence: "We found that both NfL and tau were associated with all-cause
mortality" must be changed because NfL and tau serum levels were associated with all-cause
mortality.
4- The present study demonstrated a predictive value of serum levels of NfL in all-cause mortality,
but does not correlate NfL levels with the different causes of death, in particular with mortality
associated with neurological disease.

Reviewer: Brian Gordon
Reviewer's report:
In the current work the authors retrospectively analyze blood samples take in 1997 as part of the
Memory and Morbidity in Augsburg elderly (MEMO). As part of MEMO participants underwent
neuropsychological testing and a subset had 1.5T MRI scans. They authors are interested in how
blood levels of NfL and tau are related to mortality, neuropsychological performance, and brain
atrophy and white matter lesions. The authors find that primarily NfL is related to mortality,
neuropsychological performance, and changes measured on MRI. The primary strength of the
current work is that it is being performed in a general population study and the length of follow-
up. Prior work has estimated the association of NfL, and even tau now, with MRI measures, but it
is still interesting to see what additional value can be gained by retrospectively adding new
biomarkers to a study. I have a number of points for clarification.
1.Could the authors provide more information about how WML are being quantified? The text
indicates they are being visually read. Is the reader selecting voxels that are abnormal which are
then quantified? My first thought is they were doing a reading like a Fazekas score but this seems
to be semiquantitative. You reference two prior papers from 2000 but a reader is unlikely to go
look those up to read. More information would be very helpful to the reader.
2.Given the slice thickness of your scans, how could you have WML less than 3mm in size? Also
you give the slice thickness, but not the in-plane resolution. This goes back to my first point that it
just was not clear to me how the WML values were being generated.
3.The authors start with a base model that includes age, sex, and education as predictors. They
then assess incremental models adding in additional factors of interest (e.g. NfL). Was there any
structure into how variables were entered into the model? This seems like an example were a
stepwise regression model would be appropriate, but it isn't clear what the authors did.
4.It was clear that you only imputed data when using MRI variables to predict mortality, but why
use imputation at all? What exact variables required imputation and how much of the data was
imputed? Are you imputing variables for all 117 individuals that do not have any MRI data? Did
you have enough data to actually impute any of your MRI variables accurately? Please clarify
what you did and provide justification. I may be more appropriate to simply perform the analyses
that include MRI only in the subset that actually has MRI data.

5.When performing the associations between tau/NfL and neuropsychological tests/MRI did you
include any covariates? Given the strong association NfL has with age, it would be appropriate to
include age a covariate.
6.I originally thought MRI was being summed into one aggregate measure for analyses, but it
looks like you analyzed the associations with individual regional measures as well. Did you adjust
for multiple comparisons?

Reviewer’s report
Title: Serum neurofilament light and tau as prognostic markers for all-cause mortality in the
elderly general population– an analysis from the MEMO Study
Version: 0 Date: 07 Sep 2020
Reviewer's report:
I reviewed this manuscript that describes the evaluation of demographic, clinical, MRI and
biomarkers in a cohort of individuals recruited from the general population in the 1989/90s and
evaluated in detail in 1997.
The author focused on the group aged > 65y at the time of assessment, and evaluated the inter-
relationship between variables, and the value of baseline variables in predicting mortality.
Overall the manuscript is well written, clear and easy to follow. There are several strengths of the
paper:
- I agree with the authors that there is novelty in their findings
- The long follow up time
- The multi-dimensional data: demographic, clinical (including detailed cognitive), MRI and
biological data
- The correction of regressions for age, sex, years in education
- The high quality figures
However, I have some reservations and comments that I would like the authors to address to try to
strengthen the paper further.
- The MRI methods are unusual, which is almost certainly because the MR data is quite historic,
and was performed in a pre-digital era. However, I felt there was insufficient detail in the paper to
justify/ reproduce the methods. I was unclear how the size-dependent constant was derived and
whether this was subject to any validation. I could not access the Neuroepidemiology reference for
the cortical volume measurements, and suspect others will also be unable. I would therefore
recommend the authors provide more detail on that method and its validity (is it reproducible
between observers, has it ever been validated vs more modern quantitative volume metrics?). I
also found the term "atrophy" misleading as it implies volume change, whereas the authors had a
single scan for each participant. Please consider using a more appropriate description e.g. cortical
volume. Likewise there was reference to "change" at points (e.g. lines 209 and 260), which was
also misleading. I think these points could either be addressed, or they could be better recognised
as limitations.
- Overall the discussion seemed fairly limited and could be expanded. For example, could the
authors help the reader interpret the magnitude of the effect described by a c-statistic change from
0.663 to 0.683. Some further discussion on potential limitations including MRI (above), the
degree to which the research cohort are expected to be representative of the wider "general"
population, the relevance of the associations between tau and mortality in men vs women, the
